text: We'll close out this chapter with a practical reference you'll actually reach for: the same four string operations, named differently, across all four dialects. Substring, length, position, and trim. Let's build the table.

T-SQL only knows SUBSTRING. Oracle only knows SUBSTR. MySQL and PostgreSQL are the generous ones — they accept both spellings, so code written either way tends to just work there. Same start-and-length arguments across all of them.

For length, T-SQL has LEN, Oracle and PostgreSQL both use LENGTH, and MySQL actually splits the concept in two — LENGTH counts bytes, CHAR underscore LENGTH counts characters. That distinction only bites once multi-byte text shows up, but it's there.

Position is where the argument order will trip you up if you're not paying attention. CHARINDEX on T-SQL takes the substring first, then the string. INSTR on Oracle reverses that — string first, then substring. MySQL hedges by offering both: INSTR matching Oracle's order, and LOCATE matching T-SQL's. PostgreSQL reads almost like English: POSITION of Academy IN LTV Academy.

And finally, trimming — TRIM, LTRIM, RTRIM — works identically, by name and by behavior, on every single one of these four platforms. After seven lessons of divergence, that's a nice note to end the chapter on. Next up, Chapter Four: join syntax, starting with old-style comma joins versus the ANSI join syntax you already know from T-SQL.
